paras: The threatened lynching of Smith in Todd County, Kentucky, followed the killing of a woman and her child near Guthrie on Saturday, October 27, 1888, for which her husband, described as "a colored man named Smith," was blamed in wire reports. Smith was caught after trying to drown himself and was jailed at Springfield, Tennessee, where, a dispatch said, feeling against him was so strong "that he may be lynched." No attack on him appears in the coverage, but the story ran widely as a one-paragraph wire item under headlines such as "A Negro Fiend."

The reports placed the deaths at or near Guthrie, in Todd County, Kentucky. The wire traced the trouble to "family matters," saying Smith was jealous of his wife. Most papers gave only his surname, while the Sacramento Daily Record-Union called him "B. Smith."

According to a dispatch dated at Hopkinsville on October 29, Smith "became infuriated at his wife and beat her to death" on the Saturday before. The Clarksville Evening Chronicle, the only paper to name a weapon, said he used a fence rail. Pursued by the sheriff, he picked up his small child and fled, and on reaching a barnyard he threw the child into a pond, where it drowned. When the officer tried to arrest him, Smith jumped into the water, "resolved to perish rather than be taken alive," but help was called and he was pulled out. He was then taken to the jail at Springfield, Tennessee.

The lynching threat was reported only in general terms. The fuller wire said he "may be lynched," while a shorter Guthrie version said he was taken to Springfield "to avoid lynchers." The Washington Evening Post's news digest put it more starkly: "Lynchers are after him." None of the reports names any would-be lynchers, describes a crowd at Guthrie or Springfield, or tells of an attempt on Smith.
No later report of an inquest, an indictment, a trial or Smith's fate was found.

The story spread as a single wire paragraph, in a longer version datelined Hopkinsville and shorter ones datelined Guthrie. On October 29 and 30 it appeared in papers from Washington and Alexandria to San Antonio, Memphis, Indianapolis and St. Paul. It also reached the West Coast through the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Seattle Post-Intelligencer, and weeklies were still reprinting it in mid-November.

Headlines cast Smith as a monster: the Alexandria Gazette ran "A Negro Fiend," the San Antonio Daily Light "A Fiendish Brute" and the Evening Star "A Desperate Negro Murderer." The St. Paul Daily Globe went further, heading the item "SMITH SHOULD SWING." Sacramento titled it "A Kentucky Othello," and the Seattle Post-Intelligencer made the threat itself the headline, "In Danger of Lynching."

Other versions left out the threat entirely. The Annapolis Evening Capital headed its account "Double Murder and Attempted Suicide" with no mention of lynchers, and the Clarksville Evening Chronicle gave the killings a single sentence. Every version stated Smith's guilt as fact, and none reported any statement from him or from officials.

The accounts differed mainly on details. The Evening Post's digest item said that Smith "murdered his wife and child" and that lynchers were "after him," which implies he was still at large, whereas the wire reports had him captured and jailed at Springfield. Datelines also varied, from Hopkinsville on October 29 to Guthrie on October 28, 29 or 30.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Smith in Todd County, Kentucky
bases: The only collective violence reported is a threatened lynching of a Black man accused of killing his wife and child: he 'may be lynched' (A1), was jailed 'to avoid lynchers' (A6), and 'Lynchers are after him' (A5); no attack is reported.

Smith was not killed; he was arrested and jailed at Springfield, Tenn., and the papers report only that feeling ran high and that 'lynchers' threatened him (A1, A5, A6). The threatened lynchers are unnamed and uncounted, and their pretext was the murder accusation.

Nearly every version is the same wire paragraph (A1, A6, A10 and reprints); only the Clarksville brief (A9), with its fence-rail detail, may come from a separate report, and it does not mention the lynching threat.

record_check.dossier: One person: 'Smith' ('B. Smith' in one paper). 'Lynch Smith' is not a name in any article; it appears to come from the headline 'In Danger of Lynching'.
threatened: papers report only that he 'may be lynched' or that lynchers were after him; no attempt is described
Pursuit was by the sheriff, not a mob; the mob element is a reported threat only
In jail at Springfield, Tenn., when the threat was reported (one digest line implies he was at large)
Killings in Kentucky; jail and the reported threat at Springfield, Tennessee
